steps.do: Change into the project root.
Run the Playwright spec that reads getComputedStyle on each menu item.
Check that the spec compares the computed font-size to the token value in pixels.
Confirm the spec covers both the open and the focused menu state.

K-022502.example: The computed font-size of the menu label is 16px, which equals --font-size-menu-item at 1rem with the root at 16px. The computed font-family is Inter, sans-serif, matching --font-family-ui.
K-022502.check: Expected: the spec output reports 1 passed, and the computed values equal the token values in pixels for every state.
traps: A small model often reads the CSS file and assumes the browser agrees, but only computed styles prove the cascade result.
Do not compare rem values as strings; convert to px using the root font size before comparing.
A focus or hover override can change the font weight or size, so test each state separately instead of only the resting state.

steps.do: Change into the project root.
List every font-size token defined in the token stylesheet.
Count the font-size tokens to confirm the scale has the expected number of steps.
Confirm no menu token is smaller than 0.875rem, which is 14px.

K-022503.example: The stylesheet defines 6 font-size tokens, from --font-size-xs at 0.75rem to --font-size-lg at 1.25rem. The menu item token --font-size-menu-item is 1rem, which is above the 14px floor.
K-022503.check: Expected: the count matches the documented scale of 6, and every menu token value is 0.875rem or larger.
traps: A small model may count the same token twice when it appears in a comment or a dark-theme override, so count unique names instead.
Do not treat a 12px label as acceptable for menus just because it fits; enforce the 14px floor.
Renaming a token without updating every var() reference breaks the menu silently, so search for the old name before finishing.

steps.do: Create the color asset folder for the accent color set.
Create the Swift file that exposes the color tokens.
Add Contents.json to Accent.colorset with one sRGB entry for light and one for dark appearance.
Expose the token as extension Color with static let accent set to Color with the name Accent and the module bundle.
Run the tests that load the token.

K-022504.example: The light Accent value is sRGB 0.00, 0.40, 0.80, and the dark value is 0.40, 0.70, 1.00. Color.accent resolves to the dark value when the color scheme is dark.
K-022504.check: swift test --filter ColorTokenTests prints 'Executed 2 tests, with 0 failures'.
traps: Small models hardcode Color(red:green:blue:) in views instead of using tokens.
Leaving out the dark appearance entry gives one value in both modes, so check both entries exist.

steps.do: Create the spacing token file.
Declare the base spacing as 8 points and the minimum tap height as 44 points in an enum named Spacing.
In the view, add @ScaledMetric(relativeTo: .body) var iconSize: CGFloat = 20 and apply .frame(minHeight: 44) to the row.
Set the booted simulator to the largest accessibility content size.
steps.cmd: xcrun simctl ui booted content_size accessibility-extra-extra-large

steps.do: Run the spacing snapshot tests on the simulator.

K-022505.example: At accessibility sizes the scaled icon is larger than 20 points, and the row still has a frame minHeight of 44. The tap target never drops below 44 points.
K-022505.check: xcodebuild test prints 'TEST SUCCEEDED', and SpacingTests asserts the row height is at least 44.
traps: Small models hardcode padding: 8 and skip @ScaledMetric.
Do not use .frame(height: 44), because it clips large text; use minHeight instead.

steps.do: Create the token spec test file.
Write XCTAssertGreaterThanOrEqual for the 11 point caption minimum and XCTAssertEqual for the 44 point tap size.
Write a helper that computes the WCAG contrast ratio from sRGB luminance, then assert the accent on white is at least 4.5.
Run only the token spec tests.
List the test cases to confirm all of them are discovered.

K-022506.example: The contrast helper returns about 5.6 for the accent color #0066CC on white, which passes 4.5:1. A test fails if a token change drops the ratio below 4.5.
K-022506.check: swift test --filter TokenSpecTests prints 'Executed 3 tests, with 0 failures'.
traps: Small models use XCTAssertTrue(a == b), which hides the actual value on failure.
Use XCTAssertEqual and XCTAssertGreaterThanOrEqual, and compute contrast from relative luminance, not RGB distance.

steps.do: Create the select view file.
Write a Picker with a label bound to a State value, using .font(AppFont.body), .padding(Spacing.md), and an explicit .pickerStyle.
Search the component for literal font sizes, which should return no matches.
Compile the package and confirm zero errors.
Count the snapshot test entries that reference the select, expecting at least 1.

K-022507.example: A Picker labeled Size with its selection bound to a State value uses .font(AppFont.body) and .padding(Spacing.md). The grep for size: finds nothing because the font comes from the token.
K-022507.check: grep -n size: exits with code 1 and no output, swift build prints 'Build complete!', and the grep -c count is 1 or more.
traps: Small models write .font(.system(size: 15)) inside the component, which breaks the token rule.
Set .pickerStyle explicitly, because the default style depends on context, and do not use UIKit's UIPickerView.

steps.do: Create the fonts resource folder.
Copy the font file into the resource folder.
Declare the token as Font.custom with name Inter-Regular, size 17, and relativeTo .body in the typography file.
Add the Fonts folder to the package resources in Package.swift with .process.
Run the test that resolves the font name.

K-022508.example: AppFont.bodyBrand uses Font.custom with name Inter-Regular, size 17, and relativeTo body. If the font file is missing, the resolve test fails with the name not found.
K-022508.check: swift test --filter FontTokenTests prints 'Executed 1 test, with 0 failures'.
traps: Small models use a font name without checking the file's PostScript name, so open the font to confirm it.
Leaving out relativeTo stops the custom font from scaling, and a font not listed as a package resource falls back silently.

steps.do: Print the plural categories Intl gives for English.
Print the plural categories Intl gives for Arabic, which has more forms than English.
Write one message key per category each target locale needs, and skip categories the locale never uses.
Confirm French maps the number 1 to the one category, which the plan will rely on.

K-022509.example: English prints one and other, so two forms are needed for en. Arabic prints six categories, so the plan needs zero, one, two, few, many and other for ar.
K-022509.check: The first command prints ['one','other'], the second prints six category names, and the fourth prints one.
traps: Small models assume English plural rules apply to every language. Arabic has six categories.
Do not write if count === 1 in the component. Use plural keys from the message library so each locale gets its own form.

steps.do: Find existing sort calls and localeCompare calls in the list code so the plan replaces them.
Show what the plain code-unit comparison gives for ä and z.
Show what Intl.Collator gives for German, where ä sorts before z.
Plan a $derived sorted array that builds one collator from the current $locale value and reuses it for every row.

K-022510.example: The plain comparison prints false because ä has a higher code point than z. The collator prints -1, so the plan sorts ä before z for German.
K-022510.check: The second command prints false, the third prints -1, and the first command lists every sort site in src/lib.
traps: Small models call localeCompare with no locale, which follows the system locale and changes results in tests.
Build the Intl.Collator once outside the each loop, not on every render.

steps.do: Find physical left and right CSS properties in the list source that must become logical ones.
steps.cmd: rg -n -e margin-left -e margin-right -e padding-left -e padding-right -e text-align src/lib

steps.do: Check whether the root HTML sets a dir attribute that the locale store can update.
Plan logical properties: margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, and text-align: start.
Record a minimum row height of 44px in the plan, so touch targets stay usable in both directions.
Record the baseline count of physical properties so the build stage can prove the count reaches 0.
steps.cmd: rg -c -e margin-left -e margin-right -e padding-left -e padding-right src/lib

K-022511.example: rg lists 6 matches across 3 files in src/lib, which becomes the baseline. app.html has no dir attribute, so the plan sets dir from the locale in the root layout.
K-022511.check: The first command prints file and line matches, the second prints nothing if dir is missing, and the last prints a per-file count that adds up to the baseline.
traps: Small models change text-align but forget margins and padding. Search all four physical properties.
Do not plan a fixed width for rows. Use logical spacing so Arabic layouts do not clip.

steps.do: Find hardcoded formatting calls in the list code that the plan must replace.
Show the German number format that the plan must reproduce, with a dot for thousands and a comma for decimals.
Show the day-first date format for en-GB, which the plan must support.
Plan one formatter per locale, built in a $derived value from the $locale store, and reused by every row.

K-022512.example: The number command prints 1.234.567,5 and the date command prints 07/11/2026. The plan replaces each toFixed call with one Intl.NumberFormat built from the current locale.
K-022512.check: The second command prints exactly 1.234.567,5, the third prints exactly 07/11/2026, and the first command lists each formatting call site in src.
traps: Small models call toLocaleString() with no locale, which uses the browser locale instead of the app locale.
toFixed always writes a dot decimal, so it must go in any list that shows numbers for German users.

steps.do: Change into the project root that contains the src folder.
Search the menu folder for any literal px or rem font-size value. Exit status 1 with no output is the pass result.
Count how many menu style lines use the typography token variable. Record the number for each menu style file.
Confirm the token file defines the menu item size token.
Run the menu typography test, which computes the rendered font size of each menu item and asserts it is 16px. Read the summary line.

K-022513.example: The first grep prints nothing and exits with status 1, meaning no literal sizes remain in Menu.module.css. The second grep reports 4 matching lines, one each for the menu item, label, shortcut, and group heading. The Playwright run prints a summary such as '1 passed (4.2s)'.
K-022513.check: Expected: the literal-size grep prints no lines and exits 1, the token count is at least 1 per menu style file, the token file prints a line such as --font-size-menu-item: 1rem;, and the Playwright summary reads '1 passed' with 0 failed.
traps: A small model often treats a grep with no output as a failure, but for a literal-size search no output is the passing result. Read the exit status before reporting.
Do not count px values inside comments or unrelated components; limit the search to src/components/Menu.
Do not accept a token name without checking it exists in tokens.css, because a missing variable silently falls back to the inherited size.
A passing grep does not prove the browser renders the right size. The Playwright summary must show 0 failed before reporting success.

steps.do: Change into the project root.
Run the TypeScript compiler in no-emit mode against the project config. Any error line means failure.
Confirm the tokens object is declared with as const so keys are literal types.
Confirm the menu component imports tokens from the single tokens module.
Run the token unit tests for the menu, which assert that each token key resolves to a value. Read the test count line.

K-022514.example: The compiler exits with no output after the menu component references tokens.typography.menuItem.size. If a developer writes tokens.typography.menuItmSize, tsc reports error TS2339 on that line. The Vitest run prints a line such as 'Tests 3 passed (3)'.
K-022514.check: Expected: tsc prints nothing and exits 0, grep shows as const on the tokens export line, and Vitest reports 'Tests 3 passed (3)' with 0 failed.
traps: A small model often reports success after tsc prints warnings only, but any error line means the check failed.
Without as const, a typo in a token key compiles silently, so confirm the declaration before trusting the compiler result.
Do not import token values by copying their numbers into the menu file, because that bypasses the single source of truth.
A clean tsc run does not prove runtime values are correct. The Vitest summary must show 0 failed before reporting success.

steps.do: List the duration classes the project already uses.
Locate any existing toast file so the plan matches its naming.
Plan duration-200 for enter and duration-150 for exit on the toast root.
Confirm that enter plus exit stays at or under 350ms.

K-022515.example: Enter uses duration-200 (200ms) with ease-out and exit uses duration-150 (150ms) with ease-in on the toast root. Together they total 350ms, which stays under the 400ms ceiling.
K-022515.check: The plan lists two duration values, 200 and 150, and the rg output shows no duration above duration-300 in the toast's own folder.
traps: Small models often pick duration-500 or higher because it looks smooth. Toasts should finish in 150ms to 300ms.
Do not mix duration values across enter and exit without writing them down.

steps.do: Check the Tailwind major version in package.json.
Find the stylesheet that holds the @theme block.
Write the token plan with --text-table 0.875rem and --spacing 0.25rem in docs/table-tokens.md.
Confirm the plan file exists before building.

K-022522.example: package.json shows tailwindcss ^4.1.0, so the plan puts --text-table: 0.875rem and --color-table-border: #e2e8f0 in the @theme block of src/app.css. The test command exits with status 0 once docs/table-tokens.md exists.
K-022522.check: grep prints a line such as tailwindcss ^4.1.0, rg prints src/app.css with an @theme line number, and test exits 0 with no output.
traps: Putting tokens in tailwind.config.js in a v4 project, where the @theme block in CSS is the place for them.
Writing rem values as px, which stops the table from scaling with the user's font size.
Planning tokens without a fixed list, so there is nothing to check the build against.

steps.do: Read the current cell classes in the table component.
Decide cell padding of py-3 and text-sm with leading-5 so each row is 44px tall.
Record the 44px row target and the 14px font size in docs/table-tokens.md.
Count py-3 uses in the table file to confirm the padding is applied.

K-022523.example: text-sm sets font-size 0.875rem (14px) with line-height 1.25rem (20px). py-3 adds 0.75rem (12px) top and bottom, so the row is 24px + 20px = 44px.
K-022523.check: rg -c prints 1 or more, and the planned arithmetic gives 44px in docs/table-tokens.md.
traps: Assuming text-sm uses a 1.5 line height; in Tailwind it is 1.25rem.
Mixing px-based row heights with rem padding, which makes the 44px target drift.

steps.do: List the text color classes already used in the components folder.
Plan text-slate-700 for body cells and text-slate-600 for headers, both on white.
Run the axe accessibility scan on the users table page.
Confirm the report has no color-contrast entries.

K-022524.example: slate-400 (#94a3b8) on white is about 2.6:1 and fails, while slate-600 (#475569) on white is about 7.6:1 and passes. The axe report should list zero color-contrast violations for the table.
K-022524.check: The axe run ends with a summary that lists no color-contrast rule, and the planned colors show ratios of at least 4.5:1.
traps: Using slate-400 for table text because it looks soft; it fails 4.5:1.
Applying the 3:1 large-text rule to 14px cell text, which needs 4.5:1.

steps.do: Find the cells that are right-aligned, which usually hold numbers.
Add the tabular-nums class to every numeric td so digits take equal width.
Count the lines that use tabular-nums and compare with the numeric column count.
Run the Playwright check that measures digit alignment in the amount column.

K-022525.example: The Amount column has 3 numeric cells per row, each marked with tabular-nums. rg -c prints 3 for the file and the Playwright spec reports 1 passed.
K-022525.check: rg -c matches the numeric column count, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed with exit code 0.
traps: Switching to font-mono for alignment, which changes the glyph shapes and widths of the whole cell.
Adding tabular-nums to text cells, where it has no effect and clutters the markup.

steps.do: Read the spacing setting in the stylesheet.
Plan px-4 for horizontal cell padding and py-3 for vertical padding, using the 0.25rem base step.
Build the stylesheet so the padding utilities are generated.
Count px-4 rules in the built stylesheet.

K-022526.example: With --spacing: 0.25rem, px-4 is 1rem (16px) and py-3 is 0.75rem (12px). grep -c on dist/app.css prints 1 or more when px-4 is generated.
K-022526.check: The Tailwind CLI finishes without errors, and grep -c prints a count of 1 or more.
traps: Changing --spacing without checking, which shifts every p-* and m-* utility in the app.
Using the tailwindcss bin in v4; the CLI package is @tailwindcss/cli.

steps.do: Check how the dark variant is defined in the stylesheet.
Plan dark:border-slate-700 for row borders and dark:bg-slate-800/50 for striped rows.
Record one dark color per row role in docs/table-tokens.md.
Run the Playwright check that reads computed border colors on the dark table.

K-022527.example: app.css defines @custom-variant dark (&:where(.dark, .dark *)), so dark:border-slate-700 applies inside a .dark ancestor. The Playwright spec reports 1 passed when the dark row border is #334155 on a #0f172a page.
K-022527.check: rg prints the custom-variant line, and npx playwright test prints 1 passed.

Choosing a dark stripe that drops text below 4.5:1 on the dark background.

steps.do: Search the project for transition-all, which animates every property.
Plan transition-[transform,opacity] as the only transition on the toast, and confirm the class is absent or present once.
Plan translate-x-full as the hidden state value.
Plan opacity-0 as the other hidden state value.
Count transition-all hits in the toast file, expecting zero.
Check the enter duration is 200ms by counting duration-200 hits in the toast file, expecting one.

K-022528.example: The toast uses transition-[transform,opacity] with translate-x-full and opacity-0 as its hidden state. The planned count of transition-all in the toast file is 0, and duration-200 appears once for the 200ms enter time.
K-022528.check: rg -c for transition-all prints 0 in the toast file, rg -c for duration-200 prints 1, and the plan names exactly two animated properties: transform and opacity.
traps: Small models often write transition-all because it is the first class that comes to mind. It animates width and height and causes layout cost.
Animating height on a toast causes reflow in the list below it.

steps.do: Search existing code for motion-reduce variants to match the project's pattern.
Plan motion-reduce:transition-none on the toast root so the animation is removed.
Plan motion-reduce:translate-x-0 so the toast appears in place without sliding.
Plan that the message stays visible for 4000ms even when motion is reduced.

K-022529.example: The toast root has motion-reduce:transition-none and motion-reduce:translate-x-0, and it still auto-dismisses after 4000ms. Users with reduced motion see the toast fade in place without sliding.
K-022529.check: rg prints one count of 1 for each motion-reduce class on the toast root, and grep prints one line containing 4000ms, so the plan lists exactly two motion-reduce classes.
traps: Small models often drop the reduced-motion case entirely. Every slide or scale on the toast needs a motion-reduce override.
Do not remove the toast's visibility time when motion is reduced. Only the movement should stop.

steps.do: Check which gap utilities the project already uses so the spacing matches.
Plan gap-2, which is 0.5rem or 8px, between stacked toasts.
Plan a maximum of 3 visible toasts, with the fourth queued until one closes.
Plan older toasts to shift with scale-95, which is 0.95.
Plan older toasts to shift down with translate-y-2, which is 0.5rem.

K-022530.example: Stacked toasts use gap-2 (0.5rem) between each item, and the list shows at most 3 visible toasts. Older toasts scale to 0.95 and shift down by translate-y-2.
K-022530.check: rg prints gap-2 in the plan or component, grep prints one line containing maximum of 3, and the plan states a maximum count of 3 visible toasts.
traps: Small models often allow unlimited toasts, which pushes content off screen. Cap the visible count at 3.
Do not use gap-2.5 or an arbitrary px value unless the project already uses it. Use the existing spacing scale.

steps.do: Plan ease-out for the enter animation.
Plan ease-in for the exit animation.
Plan auto-dismiss at 4000ms after the pointer leaves the toast.
Plan enter duration of 200ms or less so it matches duration-200.
List the Playwright tests that cover timing, expecting at least one.

K-022531.example: Enter uses ease-out over 200ms and exit uses ease-in over 150ms. The toast auto-dismisses 4000ms after the pointer leaves, and the timing test is listed in the Playwright output.
K-022531.check: npx playwright test --list --grep toast prints at least one test with toast in its name, and grep shows the plan states 4000ms and 200ms as numbers.
traps: Small models often set auto-dismiss below 2000ms, which users cannot read. Use 4000ms as the default for a short message.
Do not use ease-in for the entry, because it starts slow and feels laggy.

steps.do: Create the theme folder if it does not exist.
Create the token file.
Write a NavTokens class that extends ThemeExtension with final TextStyle fields selectedLabel and unselectedLabel, a const constructor, and copyWith and lerp overrides.
Confirm the class is declared exactly once in the file.
Check that the file analyzes with no issues.

K-022532.check: grep -c prints 1 and flutter analyze prints 'No issues found!'.

steps.do: Find every place the nav bar theme is built.
Confirm labelTextStyle uses WidgetStateProperty.resolveWith instead of one fixed style.
Write a labelTextStyle that returns NavTokens.selectedLabel when WidgetState.selected is present and NavTokens.unselectedLabel otherwise, with the color taken from the ColorScheme.
Analyze the nav folder.
Run the label style test.

K-022533.check: flutter analyze prints 'No issues found!' and flutter test prints 'All tests passed!'.

steps.do: Create the test file.
Write a widget test that pumps NavigationBarThemeData with height 64 and asserts tester.getSize of each NavigationDestination has width and height of at least 48.
Run the tap target test.
Confirm the 48 assertion is present in the file.

Set data-state to open or closed on the listbox element in the component.
Build the stylesheet with the Tailwind v4 CLI.
Confirm the 150ms duration class was generated.

K-022664.example: The listbox ul uses duration-150 ease-out and toggles data-state from closed to open on click. Opening sets opacity and scale to 1, and closing returns them to opacity-0 and scale-95 in 150ms.
K-022664.check: The build exits 0 and grep prints duration-150 at least once.
traps: Using display:none or the hidden class on the panel, so no transition can run.
Choosing duration-300 or longer, when a select should finish in 150ms to 200ms.
Forgetting data-state, so the closed styles never apply.

steps.do: Replace the plain transition on the listbox with motion-safe:transition-[opacity,transform] and add motion-reduce:transition-none.
Add motion-reduce:scale-100 so the panel does not scale when reduced motion is on.
Build the stylesheet.
Confirm the reduced-motion media query was emitted.
Run the Playwright test that emulates reducedMotion as reduce and reads the computed transition duration.

K-022665.example: With the OS set to reduce motion, the listbox computed transition-duration must be 0s and the open animation is skipped. Playwright's emulateMedia sets reducedMotion to reduce in the test.
K-022665.check: grep prints prefers-reduced-motion and Playwright reports 1 passed with computed transition-duration 0s.
traps: Writing a plain transition class without motion-safe, which animates for users who asked for less motion.
Using motion-safe alone and forgetting the motion-reduce fallback.
Testing only in a browser with reduced motion off, which never exercises the new branch.

steps.do: Add the class group to the button element that wraps the trigger.
Set data-state to open or closed on that button in the component.
On the chevron svg, add transition-transform duration-200 ease-out group-data-[state=open]:rotate-180.
Build the stylesheet.
Confirm the group-data rotate selector was emitted.
Run the Playwright test that clicks the trigger and reads the chevron transform.

K-022666.example: Clicking the button sets data-state to open, and the chevron rotates 180 degrees over 200ms. Closing sets data-state back to closed, and the chevron returns to 0 degrees.
K-022666.check: grep prints rotate-180 and Playwright reports 1 passed for the chevron transform test.
traps: Putting the data-state attribute on the svg instead of the group parent, so group-data never matches.
Forgetting transition-transform, so the chevron jumps instead of animating.
Using transition-all on the chevron, which animates unrelated properties too.

steps.do: Search the source folder for any transition-all class.
Replace each transition-all with transition-[opacity,transform] on the listbox and chevron.
Search again to confirm no transition-all remains.
Build the stylesheet.
Confirm the transition-property rule was emitted.

K-022667.example: The listbox had transition-all duration-150, and now it has transition-[opacity,transform] duration-150. The rg count of transition-all in src drops from 3 to 0.
K-022667.check: The second rg prints no lines and exits 1, and grep prints transition-property at least once.
traps: Writing transition-[opacity, transform] with a space, which Tailwind does not parse as one class.
Assuming rg finds nothing because the code is fine, when the class lives in a file outside the scanned folder.
Adding transition without a duration class, so the default timing applies instead of the intended one.

steps.do: List every duration class used in the select source.
Replace any duration above 200 with duration-200 or duration-150.
Re-list the duration classes to confirm only 150 or 200 remain.
Build the stylesheet so the duration classes are emitted.
Run the Playwright test that measures open and close transition durations in milliseconds.

K-022668.example: A duration-300 class on the listbox is changed to duration-150. The Playwright test asserts every transition-duration on the listbox is 150ms or 200ms.
K-022668.check: The second rg prints only duration-150 or duration-200 lines, and Playwright reports 1 passed.
traps: Using duration-500 for a fade and expecting the select to feel fast.
Ignoring arbitrary values like duration-[300ms], which the pattern duration-[0-9]+ does not match.
Measuring with transitions skipped, so the timing never actually runs.

steps.do: Create modal.html for the page.
Create modal.css beside it for the error styles.
Declare a dialog element with id confirm-modal, role set to alertdialog, and aria-labelledby set to the heading id.
Inside the dialog add a p with class error-message, role set to alert, and the hidden attribute so it starts empty and hidden.
In modal.css set .error-message color to #b00020 on a white background, which gives 7.3:1 contrast against the 4.5:1 minimum.
Count the alertdialog roles to confirm exactly one dialog is declared.

K-022669.example: The dialog is id confirm-modal with a hidden p.error-message, and when save fails JavaScript removes hidden and sets the text to 'Save failed: network timeout.' The grep count returns 1 when the dialog is declared once.
K-022669.check: grep -c prints 1 and modal.html contains role="alertdialog" exactly once.
traps: Small models often put role="alert" on the dialog instead of alertdialog.
They also leave the hidden attribute off, so an empty error line shows as a blank box.

steps.do: Create results.html containing a dialog with a ul id results-list that has no whitespace inside it.
Create results.css beside it for the empty rule.
Add the rule ul#results-list:empty::before with content 'No results found.' and color #4a4a4a, which gives 8.9:1 contrast on white.
Set the ul min-height to 3rem so the placeholder has room and is not clipped.
Check that the empty ul markup is present exactly once in the page.

K-022670.example: An empty ul id results-list renders 'No results found.' above the close button. After the script appends one li, the ::before text disappears because the element is no longer empty.
K-022670.check: grep -c prints 1 and in the browser the placeholder text is visible while the list is empty.
traps: A ul with a newline or space inside it will not match :empty, so the placeholder never shows.
Small models also forget that ::before needs content set or nothing renders.

steps.do: Add a label and an input with id email and type email inside the dialog form.
Set aria-invalid to true and aria-errormessage to email-error only when the field is invalid.
Add a span id email-error with class field-error and the text 'Enter a valid email address.' right after the input.
Set input min-height to 44px in modal.css so the touch target meets the 44px guideline.
Count the aria-invalid attributes in the markup to confirm exactly one field declares it.
Confirm the input height rule is set to 44px in the stylesheet.

K-022671.example: The email input has aria-invalid="true" and aria-errormessage="email-error" when the address fails validation. The rg count prints 1 and grep prints a line containing min-height: 44px.
K-022671.check: rg prints a count of 1 and grep prints a line containing min-height: 44px.
traps: Small models leave aria-invalid="true" on after the value is fixed, so screen readers keep reporting an error.
They also skip the min-height rule and only style the color.

steps.do: Create modal.js beside modal.html.
In modal.js add a close handler that calls dialog close, then sets the error text to empty and adds hidden back to .error-message.
Call form reset in the same handler so the input value and aria-invalid state return to defaults.
Check that the file has valid JavaScript syntax with no parse errors.
Count the addEventListener calls to confirm the close handler is attached once.

K-022672.example: After a failed save the user presses Escape, and the close handler sets the error paragraph to hidden and empties its text. Reopening the modal shows no stale error message.
K-022672.check: node --check prints nothing and exits 0, and grep -c prints 1 for one close listener.
traps: Small models only call dialog close and forget the error reset, so old errors appear on reopen.
They also attach the listener inside the open function, which stacks duplicate handlers each time.

steps.do: In modal.js set tabindex to -1 on the error paragraph so it can receive programmatic focus.
After the error text is shown and hidden is removed, call focus on the error paragraph element.
Create a tests folder for the browser tests.
Create the Playwright spec file that opens the modal, submits an empty form, and checks document.activeElement.
Run the focus test and confirm it passes.

K-022673.example: Submitting the empty form shows 'Name is required.' and moves focus to p.error-message with tabindex -1. The Playwright run reports 1 passed.
K-022673.check: npx playwright test prints '1 passed' and the test fails if document.activeElement is not the error paragraph.
traps: Small models leave tabindex off, so focus() silently does nothing.
They also call focus before removing hidden, which fails because hidden elements cannot take focus.

steps.do: Create state.css beside modal.html.
Set the dialog data-state to one of loading, empty, or error, and default it to loading.
Write the rule dialog[data-state="error"] .error-block with display block, and dialog:not([data-state="error"]) .error-block with display none.
Set the transition on .state-block opacity to 200ms, and set it to 0ms inside a prefers-reduced-motion media query.
Check that the stylesheet follows Prettier formatting with no differences.
Count the data-state attributes in the markup to confirm the dialog declares it once.

K-022674.example: The dialog starts with data-state="loading" and the script changes it to error after a failed fetch, so only the error block displays. The grep count prints 1 because only the dialog tag line in modal.html contains data-state.
K-022674.check: grep -c prints 1 and npx prettier --check reports 'All matched files use Prettier code style!'.
traps: Small models use a class toggle and a data-state attribute together, so the two sources disagree.
They also put display none on the wrong selector, which hides the loading block during an error.

steps.do: Create the UI component folder.
Create the single file component BaseButton.vue in that folder.
In script setup, declare type with defineProps defaulting to 'button' and render a native button with :type='type' and a default slot; do not use a div with role='button'.
Count the lines that open a button tag in the file; the count should be 1.
Type check the component so the SFC compiles.

K-022675.example: BaseButton.vue renders <button :type='type'> with type defaulting to 'button' so it does not submit a form by accident. Enter and Space then fire click natively, so no custom keydown handler is needed.
K-022675.check: grep prints 1 and vue-tsc exits 0 with no output.
traps: Small models often wrap a div in role='button' and add tabindex, which loses native Enter and Space handling.
Leaving type unset makes the button submit its form by default.

steps.do: Declare iconOnly as a boolean prop in defineProps and read aria-label from attrs, not from a prop.
Warn in development when iconOnly is true and useAttrs() has no aria-label, inside an if guarded by import.meta.env.DEV.
Mark the icon wrapper with aria-hidden='true' so the name comes only from the button.
List every icon-only usage in the source so each one can be checked for an aria-label.
Run the Vitest spec that renders an icon-only button and asserts its accessible name.

K-022676.example: <BaseButton icon-only aria-label='Close dialog'><XIcon aria-hidden='true' /></BaseButton> gives the button the name Close dialog. Without the label, the dev warning fires and the button has no name for screen readers.
K-022676.check: grep prints one line per icon-only usage, and Vitest reports 0 failed.
traps: Small models put aria-label on the icon instead of the button, which leaves the button unnamed.
Forgetting aria-hidden on the icon can make screen readers announce it twice.

steps.do: Declare a pressed boolean prop with default false, and declare an update:pressed emit with defineEmits.
Bind :aria-pressed='pressed' on the native button so it renders the string true or false.
In the click handler, emit update:pressed with the negated value so the parent can use v-model:pressed.
Confirm the aria-pressed binding is in the component source.
Run the spec that clicks the toggle twice and checks aria-pressed changes between true and false.

K-022677.example: The parent writes <BaseToggle v-model:pressed='muted'>Mute</BaseToggle>, and each click flips muted between true and false. The visible label stays Mute while the aria-pressed state changes.
K-022677.check: grep prints the :aria-pressed line, and Vitest reports 0 failed with the attribute reading 'false' and then 'true'.
traps: Small models change the label text to Muted instead of using aria-pressed, which breaks a stable accessible name.
Passing undefined instead of false removes the attribute, so the button loses its pressed state.

steps.do: Declare disabled and loading as boolean props with default false in defineProps.
Bind the native disabled attribute only to the disabled prop, and bind aria-disabled='true' for loading without the native attribute.
Set :aria-busy='loading' on the button and return early in the click handler when disabled or loading is true.
Confirm the aria-busy binding is in the component source.
Run the spec that checks a loading button keeps document.activeElement and does not emit click.

K-022678.example: <BaseButton :loading='saving'>Save</BaseButton> keeps focus on the button and sets aria-busy='true' while saving. A disabled button uses the native disabled attribute, which removes it from the Tab order.
K-022678.check: grep prints the aria-busy line, and Vitest reports 0 failed.
traps: Native disabled removes focus, so a button that starts a request can drop the keyboard user's place.
aria-disabled alone does not block clicks, so the handler must check the flag.

steps.do: Search the component styles for outline rules to find any outline none that hides focus.
Replace outline none with a .base-button:focus-visible rule that sets outline 2px solid and outline-offset 2px.
Pick a focus color with at least 3:1 contrast against both the button background and the page background.
Lint the component file to catch template and style rule errors.
Run the Playwright test that tabs to the button and checks the focused style has a visible outline.

K-022679.example: .base-button:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #1d4ed8; outline-offset: 2px; } gives about 6.7:1 contrast on a white page, which passes the 3:1 target. Mouse clicks skip the ring because :focus-visible matches keyboard focus.
K-022679.check: grep shows a focus-visible rule and no outline none line, eslint exits 0 with no output, and Playwright reports 0 failed.
traps: Removing outline with no replacement deletes the only focus cue.
Using :focus alone shows the ring after mouse clicks too, so use :focus-visible.

steps.do: Import useId from vue and call const hintId = useId() in script setup.
Bind :aria-describedby='hintId' on the button and render a paragraph with :id='hintId' right after it.
Keep the hint in the DOM when it is only visually hidden, using a clip class instead of v-if or display none.
Confirm the aria-describedby binding is in the component source.
Type check the component to confirm useId is imported correctly.

K-022680.example: const hintId = useId() gives each button instance its own id, so two BaseButton instances on one page do not collide. The button's :aria-describedby='hintId' points to the paragraph with :id='hintId', so the hint is read after the button name.
K-022680.check: grep prints the aria-describedby line, and vue-tsc exits 0 with no output.
traps: Hard-coded ids like 'hint' collide when the button appears twice, so use useId.
Putting the hint inside the button text makes it part of the accessible name instead of a description.

steps.do: Find every file that builds a list using ListView, GridView, or ListTile.
Count list builder call sites per file so the plan has a fixed total.
Write one plan line per list with its row count and the current row height in logical pixels.
Mark every row under 48 logical pixels tall as needing a fix.
Run the analyzer to record the baseline before any edit.

K-022681.example: rg -l prints lib/inbox/inbox_list.dart, so the plan records 1 list with 12 rows at 40 logical pixels to raise to 48. Run flutter analyze first and expect it to print No issues found! before any edit starts.
K-022681.check: rg prints each matching path once with a count line, and flutter analyze ends with 'No issues found!' before any edit.
traps: Small models assume ListTile is always large enough, but a custom Row-based row often measures 32 or 40 logical pixels.
Counting from memory misses files, so count with rg instead.
A row only passes if its tappable child is also at least 48 logical pixels, not just the outer row.

steps.do: Find deprecated textScaleFactor uses in list code so they are replaced.
Plan to read the scale with MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context) instead.
Set the test scales to 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 and record them in the plan.
Set the maximum row height so a row at 2.0 scale still fits in 3 lines without clipping.
Run the analyzer to confirm no deprecated API warnings exist before work starts.

K-022682.example: The plan uses MediaQuery.textScalerOf(context) and tests three scales, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0, on the 12-row inbox list. A baseline rg of textScaleFactor returns no lines, so no migration is needed.
K-022682.check: rg prints nothing for textScaleFactor, and dart analyze ends with 'No issues found!'.
traps: Small models use the old MediaQuery.textScaleFactorOf, which is deprecated in current Flutter.
Testing only 1.0 misses the clipping that appears at 2.0.
Do not hard code row heights, because fixed heights clip scaled text.

steps.do: Create the accessibility test folder so the new test has a home.
Confirm flutter_test is declared in pubspec.yaml so the guideline matchers can be imported.
Plan one test per guideline: androidTapTargetGuideline, iOSTapTargetGuideline, labeledTapTargetGuideline, and textContrastGuideline.
Write in the plan that each guideline runs on a pumped list with at least 3 rows.
Record the expected pass output as All tests passed! for the planned file.

K-022683.example: The plan creates test/a11y/list_a11y_test.dart, which calls expect(tester, meetsGuideline(labeledTapTargetGuideline)) on a list of 3 rows. Running flutter test on that file must print All tests passed!.
K-022683.check: mkdir -p creates test/a11y with no error, and rg prints a line showing flutter_test under dev_dependencies in pubspec.yaml.
traps: Small models forget tester.ensureSemantics(), so the semantics tree is empty and the checks pass for the wrong reason.
Treating meetsGuideline as optional lets the build pass when rows break.
androidTapTargetGuideline and iOSTapTargetGuideline check different sizes, so one does not replace the other.

steps.do: Check that the form stylesheet sets a font size for input, select, and textarea.
Run the Playwright spec that reads computed font size for every form control.
Confirm the summary shows no failed tests and every control is at least 16px.

K-022684.example: The grep line shows font-size: 1rem for input, select, and textarea. The spec prints 3 passed, with each control computed at 16px.
K-022684.check: Playwright prints 3 passed and 0 failed, and grep lists a 1rem or 16px rule covering all three control types.
traps: Setting 15px or 0.9rem passes a visual check but still triggers focus zoom on iOS.
Testing only input and skipping select or textarea leaves two control types unchecked.
Reading the CSS source alone misses overrides, so the spec must check computed style.

steps.do: Confirm the Playwright config file exists in the project root.
Run the latency spec, which types 20 characters into the email field and times each keystroke with performance.now.
Read the printed maximum keystroke time from the spec output.

K-022685.example: The spec types 20 characters into input#email under 4x CPU throttling and prints max 84ms. A validator that runs a slow regex on every key would print a value above 200ms and fail.
K-022685.check: Playwright prints 1 passed, and the reported maximum keystroke time is below 200ms, for example 84ms.
traps: Timing a single keystroke misses slow handlers, so the spec must loop over at least 20 characters.
Running on a fast laptop hides the cost, so the spec must enable 4x CPU throttling.
A debounced validator hides the handler cost, so the spec must measure with debounce turned off.

steps.do: Build the project so the minified form script is written to dist.
Confirm the minified form script exists in dist.
Print the minified file size in bytes.
Compare the printed size against the budget of 10240 bytes.

K-022686.example: The build writes dist/form.min.js, and stat prints 7312. That is under the 10240 byte budget, so the card passes.
K-022686.check: stat prints a number at or below 10240, for example 7312, and the test -f command exits without error.
traps: Measuring the source file instead of the minified output gives a far larger number than the budget applies to.
Mixing up 10KB, 10 kB, and 10000 bytes shifts the budget, so use exactly 10240 bytes.
Skipping the build leaves stat reading an older file, so always rebuild before measuring.

steps.do: Count the input lines in the contact form, assuming one input element per line.
Count the lines that declare an autocomplete attribute.
Run the Playwright spec that asserts every input has an autocomplete value other than off.

K-022687.example: contact.html has four inputs named name, email, tel, and postal. grep -c prints 4 for both the input count and the autocomplete count, and the spec passes.
K-022687.check: The two grep counts are equal, for example 4 and 4, and Playwright prints 1 passed.
traps: Setting autocomplete="off" on every field blocks autofill, so use real tokens such as email or tel.
Counting submit buttons or hidden inputs inflates the total, so count only visible fields.
Checking only the first input misses the rest, so the spec must loop over all inputs.

steps.do: Find existing Semantics wrappers in list code so the plan does not duplicate them.
Decide the spoken label order as title, then subtitle, then status, and write it in the plan.
Wrap each row content in MergeSemantics so the title and subtitle read as one node.
Mark only decorative icons with ExcludeSemantics so they are not announced.
Count the rows that will be merged so a later test can check the number.
Run the accessibility test folder and expect each row label test to pass with the exact planned strings, such as 'Invoice 42, due Friday, unread'.

K-022688.example: Each inbox row reads as 'Invoice 42, due Friday, unread' from one MergeSemantics node, with the chevron icon excluded. The plan lists 9 row widgets to merge, which must match the rg -c total of 9.
K-022688.check: rg -n shows the existing wrappers with line numbers, the row count in the plan matches the rg -c total, and flutter test exits with status 0 when all row label tests pass.
traps: Small models wrap the whole ListView in MergeSemantics, which merges every row into one node and hides them from the reader.
ExcludeSemantics on a wrapper that holds the tappable area removes that row from accessibility, so exclude only the icon.
Do not invent a label order without writing it down, since the test later checks that exact string.

steps.do: Find every hard coded color in list widgets so each text and background pair is on the plan.
Write the minimum ratio of 4.5 to 1 for body text under 18.66 pixels bold or 24 pixels regular.
Write the minimum ratio of 3 to 1 for large text at or above those sizes.
List each text and background pair with its computed ratio in the plan.
Confirm the planned contrast test file path is free before writing it.

K-022689.example: Subtitle text Color(0xFF757575) on a white background measures about 4.6 to 1, which passes the 4.5 to 1 minimum. The plan marks any pair under 4.5 to 1 as failing and sets a new color before build.
K-022689.check: rg prints each Color line with its file and line number, and every body text pair in the plan has a ratio of 4.5 or higher. test -e exits with status 1 when the file path is free.
traps: Small models assume a light grey looks readable, but many greys fail 4.5 to 1 on white.
The 3 to 1 minimum applies only at the stated large sizes, so do not use it for body text.
Rely on the measured ratio, not a visual check.

steps.do: Create the golden folder so the planned image files have a location.
List the three states to capture as list_default.png, list_focus.png, and list_text_scale_2x.png in the plan.
Check that no golden files already exist so none are overwritten by accident.
Plan an exact matchesGoldenFile call for each state, since flutter_test compares pixels.
Count the planned matchesGoldenFile calls in the test folder and expect exactly 3.
Write the expected golden file count of 3 into the plan and confirm the folder is empty first.

K-022690.example: The plan lists list_default.png, list_focus.png, and list_text_scale_2x.png under test/goldens. A find run returns no PNG files, so the baseline count is 0 and the planned count is 3. The rg -c run on test/a11y returns 3 matches.
K-022690.check: find prints no lines and ls -1 test/goldens prints nothing before any golden is created. rg -c prints 3 for the planned matchesGoldenFile calls.
traps: Small models run flutter test --update-goldens during planning, which writes baseline images before the states are decided.
A golden compares pixels exactly, so any font or device change will fail it.
Image names with spaces or capitals break later diffs.

steps.do: List every script tag in the contact page.
Run a Lighthouse performance audit on the built contact form page and save the report.
Count the items in the render-blocking resources audit.

K-022691.example: The grep shows the form script tag has defer, and jq prints 0. Before the change, the same audit listed 1 item for /js/form.js loaded without defer in head.
K-022691.check: jq prints 0 for the render-blocking audit count.
traps: Adding defer to an inline script does nothing, because defer only applies to scripts with a src attribute.
Reading a cached report from before the edit gives a false zero, so rerun Lighthouse after each change.
Moving a script to the end of body without running the audit can still leave render-blocking CSS in head.

steps.do: List every font token line in tokens.css to see what is defined.
Count the font tokens, which should be exactly four: size-sm, size-base, weight-semibold, and line-height-tight.
Find any literal font-size, font-weight, or line-height value in tabs.css that does not use var().
Run the Playwright spec that checks the computed font properties of each tab.

K-022692.example: tokens.css sets --font-size-sm: 0.875rem and --font-weight-semibold: 600, and tabs.css uses font-size: var(--font-size-sm) on .tab. The count of tokens is 4 and the literal-value count is 0, so the stylesheet is fully tokenized.
K-022692.check: grep -c prints 4, the literal-value grep prints 0, and Playwright reports '1 passed' or more with no failures.
traps: A small model often counts the lines with a plain grep and forgets that comments can also match the pattern. Confirm the matches are real declarations.
Literal values such as line-height: 1.25 contain digits and must be flagged. Do not assume every var() line is correct without checking the count.

steps.do: Count hex color literals in css/tabs.css, which should be zero because colors belong in tokens.css.
Print the line numbers of any hex literal so the offending declaration can be fixed.
Confirm the token file defines the color tokens the tabs use, such as --color-text-muted.
Check that the stylesheet is formatted with Prettier after the edit.

K-022693.example: tabs.css originally had color: #595959 on .tab, which the count catches as 1. After replacing it with color: var(--color-text-muted), the count drops to 0.
K-022693.check: The first grep prints 0, the second prints no lines, and Prettier reports 'All matched files use Prettier code style!'.
traps: Hex colors can also appear inside rgb() or hsl() literals, so a hex-only grep is not enough. Search for rgb( and hsl( too.
A count of 0 proves nothing if the file path is wrong. Confirm css/tabs.css exists before trusting the output.

steps.do: Start the local page server in the project directory so the tabs page is reachable.
Run the axe CLI against the tabs page limited to WCAG 2.0 AA rules.
Confirm the color-contrast rule reports no violations in the axe output.
Compute the ratio for the muted tab color #595959 on #ffffff by hand, which should be about 7.0:1.

K-022694.example: The unselected tab text color #595959 on a #ffffff background gives a ratio of about 7.0:1, which passes the 4.5:1 minimum for 16px text. The selected label #1a1a1a gives about 17.4:1.
K-022694.check: The axe command exits with code 0 and prints no color-contrast violations, and the hand-computed ratio for each tab label is at least 4.5:1.
traps: A small model often reports a pass after axe runs without checking the output for the color-contrast rule. Read the rule list, not only the exit code.
Axe cannot test text drawn over a background image or a gradient reliably. Measure those labels by hand against the lightest background point.

steps.do: Confirm the token --tab-min-height is defined in tokens.css with the value 44px.
Check that tabs.css applies the token as min-height on the tab element.
Run the Playwright spec that measures each tab bounding box and asserts height of at least 44px.

K-022695.example: tokens.css sets --tab-min-height: 44px and tabs.css sets min-height: var(--tab-min-height) on [role=tab]. The spec measures a rendered tab at 46px, which passes the 44px threshold.
K-022695.check: The token grep prints one line containing 44px, the tabs grep prints one line, and Playwright reports 'passed' with every measured tab height at or above 44.
traps: Setting a height on the parent tablist does not guarantee each tab meets the target. Measure each tab element directly.
A small model may read 44 as a unitless number. The value must be 44px, and a 44px minimum counts only on the rendered box.

steps.do: Count px font-size declarations in css/tabs.css, which should be zero.
Print any px font-size declarations with line numbers so they can be converted to rem.
Run the Playwright spec that asserts the computed tab font-size equals 16px at the default root size.

K-022696.example: A rule with font-size: 14px is replaced by font-size: var(--font-size-sm), where the token is 0.875rem. With the root at 16px, the computed size is 14px and the count returns 0.
K-022696.check: The count prints 0, the second grep prints no lines, and Playwright reports the computed font-size as 14px for .tab with no failures.
traps: Computed font-size is always in px in the browser, so checking it alone does not prove rem was used. Check the source with grep too.
